claims.text: Controlled alloying with secondary transition metals can spatially isolate noble-metal active sites.
Formation of isolated noble-metal sites governs the enhanced performance of the ethanol-oxidation catalyst.
Alloying and noble-metal site isolation modulate the surface electronic structure.
Alloying shifts the d-band center of isolated noble-metal sites.
The alloying-induced electronic shift weakens adsorption of poisoning intermediates such as CO.
Weaker adsorption of poisoning intermediates enhances catalytic activity and suppresses deactivation.
Electronic modulation at isolated sites facilitates the complete 12-electron/12-proton ethanol-oxidation pathway.
The unalloyed nanoscale PGM catalyst contains aggregated PGM sites with strong inter-site interactions.
The unalloyed PGM catalyst has a tendency to undergo CO poisoning.
A moderate, optimal degree of alloying will produce a higher ethanol-oxidation current density than the pure PGM baseline.
An optimal degree of alloying will increase selectivity toward complete ethanol oxidation to CO2 rather than partial products such as acetaldehyde.
An optimal degree of alloying will improve cycling durability relative to the pure PGM baseline.
The pure PGM baseline has lower activity, selectivity, and durability because of stronger poisoning and inefficient electron transfer.
Excessive alloying may disrupt the crystalline structure and reduce catalytic performance.
A secondary metal that is unstable under the reaction conditions may cause performance to decline.
The optimal alloying ratio may vary with the particular PGM and operating environment.
